Thursday, 14 December, nine in the morning. Before the concert at the regional council, a journalist from a local radio station interviews Julien by phone.
Good morning, Monsieur Moreau. Thank you for joining us. Today is the big day: the vote on the regional budget and your orchestra’s concert in front of the councillors.
Good morning. Yes, it’s an important day. Especially for the children. Since this concert was announced, they’ve talked about nothing else.
Let’s remind our listeners what this is about. The "Musique en partage" project is asking for funding for a free orchestra and the construction of a rehearsal room in La Duchère.
That’s right. Since the orchestra was created in September, we’ve been running on donations. Forty-seven instruments, given by the people of Lyon.
And a petition too. There’s talk of more than five thousand signatures. How do you explain such support?
I think people have seen the children’s joy. And the parents’ pride. It isn’t just music, it’s self-confidence, patience, teamwork.
Some councillors, however, talk of a luxury in a time of crisis. What do you say to them?
I invite them to come and listen. Ten minutes. After listening, they’ll decide. I trust their judgement.
What time is the result expected to be announced?
The concert is at eleven, the vote right after. The result should be known before noon.
A word about your musicians? They say the youngest is seven and the oldest of your supporters is eighty-six.
(laughs) It’s true. She had a cold, but her doctor gave his permission last night. She’ll be in the front row. Her presence means a lot to us.
Thank you, Monsieur Moreau, and good luck. We’ll follow the vote live, and we’ll announce the result in our midday news.
Thank you. And to all the listeners who signed the petition: thank you for your generosity.
is about ("il s’agit de" = it’s about)
"-syohn": construction = "kohn-strewk-syohn". The nasal "ohn" at the end.
"-mahn": financement = "fee-nahns-mahn". The final t is silent.
Nominalisation means turning a verb or an adjective into a NOUN. Written French (the press, administration, universities) uses it a lot, because it makes sentences shorter and more "objective":
On annoncera le résultat à midi.
Romanian does the same: "a adopta → adoptarea", "a anunța → anunțul" (like English "adopt → adoption"). So nominalisation is easy to understand; the hard part is just choosing the right suffix.
financer → le financement, juger → le jugement
nettoyer → le nettoyage, laver → le lavage
naître → la naissance, présent → la présence
Gender tip: almost all nouns in -tion, -sion, -ure, -ée, -ance are FEMININE; those in -ment and -age are MASCULINE.
Some verbs give "short" nouns, with no suffix or with an irregular form. They have to be learned as vocabulary:
fier → la fierté, beau → la beauté, généreux → la générosité
grand → la grandeur, doux → la douceur
jeune → la jeunesse, triste → la tristesse
franc → la franchise, gourmand → la gourmandise
patient → la patience, présent → la présence
All these nouns are FEMININE: "la fierté", "la grandeur" (note that "le courage" is an exception — it comes from "cœur" and is masculine).
French headlines very often use the NOMINAL construction, with no conjugated verb:
Construction of a rehearsal room in La Duchère.
Pride and emotion at the regional council.
To understand a headline, turn it into a verbal sentence: "Adoption du budget" = "Le budget a été adopté."
Le vote du budget et un concert
Combien de signatures a la pétition ?
À quelle heure est le concert ?
Quel âge a le plus jeune musicien ?

How do you explain such support?

On Thursday 14 December, at eight in the morning, a coach pulled up outside the school in La Duchère. Thirty-six children were waiting on the pavement, with their instruments, their plastic buckets and their parents, who had all taken the morning off. It was cold. Nobody complained.

The driver was a man of about sixty, with a big moustache. Seeing the children climb in with their violins, he turned up the radio. It was Julien’s interview, as it happened. The children shouted with joy when they heard their teacher’s voice through the speaker.

Julien was sitting in the front row, next to Claire Vasseur, trying not to show his nerves. Behind him, Radu and Lucia were counting the children for the third time. Inès was clutching Lucien Roux’s clarinet to her chest. Yanis said nothing. He was looking out of the window, very pale.

The regional headquarters was a large modern building, all glass, on the banks of the Rhône. The children had never seen anything like it. In the huge entrance hall, their voices echoed as in a cathedral. An usher in a dark suit came to fetch them and took them to a small room to wait.

That was where Hélène arrived, in her wheelchair pushed by Odile. She was wearing her wedding hat and, under her coat, the grandmother’s embroidered ie. She was still a little pale from her cold, but her eyes were shining. Madame Roux and Madame Lambert followed in the care home minibus.

The children rushed towards her. They all knew her: she was the petition lady, the one who never let anyone leave without a signature. Hélène kissed them one by one. Then she looked at Yanis, still just as pale, and beckoned him over.

"Are you scared?" she asked him softly. Yanis nodded. "I was scared too, at your age. I had to recite a poem in front of the whole school. Do you know what I did? I picked one single person in the room, and I recited for them. Only for them."

"And who did you pick?" asked Yanis. Hélène smiled. "A boy in the front row called Henri. He was twelve and had big ears." Yanis laughed despite himself. Then he asked whether he could pick her, today. Hélène said she would be very proud.

At eleven o’clock sharp, the usher came to fetch them. The debating chamber was huge, with rows of red seats arranged in a semicircle. A hundred and fifty councillors were seated; some were reading their files, others were looking at their phones. A few looked up with curiosity when they saw thirty-six children walk in with buckets.

The president of the council introduced the project in two sentences, in a monotonous voice. Then he gave the floor to Julien. Julien stood up. He had prepared a short speech, but looking at the rows of indifferent councillors, he changed his mind. He simply said: "They’re going to play. Listen to them. Then you’ll decide."

He turned to the children and raised his arms. Silence fell over the chamber. Even those looking at their phones raised their eyes. Then the orchestra began. It was the same piece as on 15 September, but it sounded nothing like it had at the inauguration.

Three months of rehearsals had changed everything. The violins no longer squeaked. The flutes came in at the right moment. Radu’s buckets kept time with astonishing precision. And in the middle, Inès’s clarinet sang its little phrase, clear and confident, as Lucien would have played it, but in tune.

Then came Yanis’s solo. The other instruments fell silent. He was alone with his red-wood cello, in front of a hundred and fifty strangers. Julien saw his hands trembling. Then Yanis looked up, searched for Hélène in the front row, and found her. She was smiling at him.

He played for her. Only for her. Eight bars, then sixteen, because Julien had lengthened the solo the week before without telling anyone. The sound of the cello filled the chamber, deep and warm, like a human voice. In the rows, nobody moved any more.

When the last note faded, there was a long silence. A silence so deep you could hear the ventilation. Then, at the back of the chamber, an old opposition councillor, who had voted against every culture budget for twenty years, stood up and began to applaud.

The others followed him, one by one, then all together. The applause lasted almost two minutes. The children looked at each other in disbelief. Inès was crying. Yanis was searching for his parents in the audience, and when he saw his father standing, arms raised, he finally smiled.

The children left the chamber to make way for the vote. They waited in the small room with the parents, the residents, Radu, Lucia and Claire. Nobody spoke. Julien paced up and down. Hélène, in her wheelchair, held Madame Roux’s hand. Odile looked at the clock every thirty seconds.

After twenty minutes that felt like two hours, the door opened. It was the Mayor of Lyon. He looked very serious. He came over to Julien and Claire, looked at the children, then said in a grave voice: "Ninety-eight votes for. Fifty-two against. The budget is adopted."

There was a second of silence while everyone took it in. Then an explosion of joy. The children yelled, jumped, banged on their buckets. The parents hugged each other. Claire Vasseur sat down on a chair and started laughing and crying at the same time. Radu lifted Lucia up in his arms.

The mayor added, more quietly, in Julien’s ear: "The old gentleman who applauded first is the one who tipped the vote. He convinced about twenty colleagues in his group. He told me he had learned the cello as a child, and had given up because his parents thought it was useless."

Julien looked around for Hélène. She was in the middle of the room, surrounded by children who all wanted to kiss her at once. She was laughing, her hat askew. When she caught Julien’s eye, she gave him a little wave, as if to say: you see, I told you so.

On the coach home, the children sang the whole way. The driver with the moustache put on the radio. It was the midday news. The journalist announced: "Regional budget adopted for the Musique en partage project. Creation of three orchestras and construction of a rehearsal room in La Duchère."

The whole coach applauded. Yanis asked Julien what "construction of a room" meant. Julien explained that next year they would have a real room, just for them, with walls that didn’t echo and no basketballs against the door. "And Radu is going to design it," he added.

Radu went red to the tips of his ears. Lucia kissed him on the cheek in front of everyone, which set off shouts and whistles all over the coach. Inès asked whether the new room would have a corner for the buckets. Radu solemnly promised it would have the finest bucket corner in all of France.

In the evening there was an impromptu party in the Salle Henri Bernard at Fourvière. The residents had made cakes. Monsieur Mansouri had brought his oud, and Mihaela her țambal. The children played their piece again for the residents, then everyone danced, even those who could no longer walk.

Around nine, Julien found Hélène alone by the window, looking at the lights of the city. She looked exhausted, but happy. He sat down next to her. For a long time they said nothing. Below, Lyon was sparkling, with its two rivers and its Christmas lights.

"You know, Julien," she said at last, "when you found that waltz in the piano two years ago, I thought my life was over. I was waiting. I didn’t even know for what any more. And then you came, you and Ioana. And look at everything that has happened."

She pointed at the room behind them: the children dancing with the residents, Odile laughing with Madame Mansouri, Radu twirling Lucia, Mihaela striking her țambal, Yanis and his father playing together in a corner. "A room bearing Henri’s name, full of children. He would never have dared to dream of it."

Julien took her hand. It was cold and very light. "Now," she murmured, "I think I’ll be able to rest a little. Not right away, don’t worry. I want to see Rose-Hélène walk. And I want to see Radu’s room. But a little." Julien didn’t know what to say. He just held her hand tighter.

The next morning, the local paper’s front page read: "Budget adopted: music wins". Under the headline, a large photo showed Yanis playing the cello in the chamber. And in the front row, blurred but recognisable, an old lady in a hat, smiling like a girl of twenty.

Adoption du budget : la musique gagne
Lyon, 15 December. Emotion and pride yesterday at the regional council, after the budget for the "Musique en partage" project was adopted by 98 votes to 52.
Before the vote, thirty-six children from La Duchère gave a ten-minute concert in the chamber. Their arrival, with violins, clarinets and plastic buckets, caused astonishment among many councillors.
The cello solo by a ten-year-old boy was followed by a long silence, then by applause. Several opposition councillors admitted their surprise at the quality of the performance.
The funding provides for the creation of three new orchestras in the region, the purchase of instruments and the construction of a rehearsal room in La Duchère. Work should begin in the spring.

For Claire Vasseur, director of the Conservatoire, this decision is "recognition of the work of the children, the parents and all the residents who supported the project with their donations and their signatures".
In the front row, an eighty-six-year-old spectator did not hide her joy. Asked about her role in the petition, she simply replied: "I’m old, but not old enough to keep quiet."
